Keywords: Electrochemical reduction Carbon dioxide Gas-diffusion electrode Copper oxide Methanol
Gas-diffusion electrodes are prepared with commercial Cu2O and Cu2O–ZnO mixtures deposited onto carbon papers and evaluated for the continuous CO2 gas phase electroreduction in a filter-press electrochemical cell. The process mainly produced methanol, as well as small quantities of ethanol and n-propanol. The analysis includes the evaluation of key variables with effect in the electroreduction process: current density (j = 10–40 mA cm 2), electrolyte flow/area ratio (Qe/A = 1 –3 ml min 1 cm 2) and CO2 gas flow/area ratio (Qg/A = 10–40 ml min 1 cm 2), using a 0.5 M KHCO3 aqueous solution. The maximum CO2 conversion efficiency to liquid-phase products was 54.8% and 31.4% for Cu2O and Cu2O/ZnO-based electrodes at an applied potential of 1.39 and 1.16 V vs. Ag/AgCl, respectively. Besides, the Cu2O/ZnO electrodes are expected to catalyze the CO2 electroreduction for over 20 h. These results may provide new insights into the application of gas diffusion electrodes to alleviate mass transfer limitations in electrochemical systems for the transformation of CO2 to alcohols.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Carbon dioxide (CO2) concentration in the atmosphere is increasing each year by about 2 mg l 1, continuing the inexorable rise toward 400 mg l 1 and beyond [1]. In the 21st century our world is still searching for strategies to overcome the challenges associated with climate change, as well as the dependency on fossil fuels and limited natural resources.
A variety of technologies to reduce CO2 emissions have been applied through different methods. Carbon Capture and Storage (CCS) has received considerable attention as one of the technologies to handle large quantities of CO2 emissions [2], where CO2 capture seems to be the bottleneck step where the efforts have to be applied [3,4]. Nevertheless, CCS technology development has progressed slower than anticipated in large-scale demonstration plants due to the several remaining shortcomings (i.e. technological limitations, environmental and safety concerns, as well as the lack of a positive public opinion). Thus, new approaches to mitigate carbon output from the use of fossil fuels, as well as methods to fully exploit carbon neutral renewable energy sources, are needed. A possible approach to slow down the increase in atmospheric CO2 levels is the application of electrochemical methods in a Carbon
Capture and Utilization (CCU) approach. This technology is green and efficient, and has aroused intense attention worldwide recently, but there is an intense discussion on its potential since the global demand for products does not have the capacity to sequester enough CO2 emissions to significantly contribute to achieve the reduction targets [5]. However, it is also logical to consider that converting part of the captured CO2 into value-added chemicals or fuels can perfectly complement the storage of huge quantities of CO2 achieved with CCS technologies [6].
The electrochemical reduction of CO2 cannot only offer a viable route to reuse CO2, but also an excellent future option to store intermittent energy from renewable sources, allowing the storage of electrical energy in the form of chemical bonds. There are a number of valuable products that can be produced from the electroreduction of CO2 molecule, such as carbon monoxide (CO), formic acid (HCOOH), formaldehyde (CH2O), methanol (CH3OH), methane (CH4), ethanol (C2H6O), ethylene (C2H4) or n-propanol (C3H8O) [7–9]. Particularly, the challenges for converting CO2 into CH3OH are great, but the potential rewards are also enormous, since CH3OH possesses a relatively high energy density and it is a vital intermediate for several bulk chemicals used in day-today life products such as silicone, paints and plastics [7,10].
Furthermore, most electrodes used in the electroreduction of CO2 are in the form of metal plates, metal granules or electrodeposited metals on a substrate [8]. However, owing to the relatively
thanol,
low solubility of CO2 in water under ambient conditions, the reaction rates and current densities of CO2 electroreduction are limited by the mass transfer of CO2 from the bulk to the solid electrode surface [11,12]. To improve the reduction process, gas diffusion electrodes (GDEs) have been proposed to alleviate mass transport limitations across the gas–liquid interface and to the catalyst surface [13–16]. A GDE is a porous composite electrode usually composed of polymer bonded catalyst particles and a carbon support. GDEs can be operated at higher current densities (200–600 mA cm 2). Besides, because of their high porosity and partial hydrophobicity, GDEs form a characteristic gas–solid–liquid three-phase interface, which allows a homogeneous distribution over the catalyst surface. These properties make GDEs especially suitable for CO2 electroreduction in gas phase.
While significant research efforts have focused on the development of new catalyst materials, considerably fewer efforts have focused on the study of these catalysts after immobilization in GDEs. In the same manner, the literature on the application of GDEs for the electrochemical transformation of CO2 to CH3OH is scarce [17–20]. Schwartz et al. [17] firstly studied perovskitetype crystal structures (A1.8A00.2CuO4, A = La, Pr and Gd; A0 = Sr and Th) in GDE for the electrochemical reduction of CO2 under ambient conditions. The results showed that perovskite-type electrocatalysts could achieve cumulative Faradaic efficiencies for CO2 reduction to CH3OH, C2H6O, and C3H8O up to 40% at current densities of 180 mA cm 2. In 2012, Aeshala et al. [18] developed Cu2Obased GDEs by electroplating the metal particles onto a carbon paper. These materials were settled in a reactor with different solid polymer electrolytes (i.e. SPEEK, Nafion, PVA, Amberlist) for continuous gas phase CO2 electroreduction. The maximum Faradaic efficiencies were 0.54%, 0.42%, 0.3%, and 4.5% for CH3OH, HCHO, CO and CH4 production, respectively. The same group reported in 2013 a Faradaic efficiency as high as 45%, at a current density of 5.4 mA cm 2, when applying an anionic solid polymer electrolyte membrane, with CH3OH as the main liquid product, and CH4 and C2H4 as major gaseous products. They concluded that the quaternary ammonium group in the solid polymer membrane, as well as the alleviated CO2 mass transfer limitation, might have increased the efficiency of the GDE system [19]. Recently Lan et al. [20] investigated the electrochemical reduction of CO2 on a Cu(core)/CuO(shell) catalyst in a flow reactor. This catalyst predominantly produces CO and HCOOH at 54.6 mA cm 2, with a Faradaic efficiency of 21.5% and 20.2%, respectively. However, a small amount of CH3OH was also produced in the process ( 2.5% Faradaic efficiency).
Moreover, Cu and Cu/Zn-based catalysts have been conventionally applied in industrial reactions such as water gas-shift (WGS) and reverse water–gas shift (RWGS) reactions, and CH3OH production (from H2/CO/CO2) at elevated temperatures (400–600 K) and pressures (5–10 MPa) [21–23]. The application of Cu-based materials in electrochemistry, however, may be advantageous since the process can be operated at room temperature and offers a convenient method to store electrical energy without increasing CO2 emissions. Specifically, the literature demonstrated the good stability and notable catalytic ability of Cu2O-based surfaces for electrochemical hydrocarbons and/or alcohols formation from CO2 [8,11,17–20,24–28]. Besides, the inclusion of ZnO may be the key for maintaining catalytic activity, since ZnO strengthens the Cu–CO link, increasing the selectivity to alcohols, and stabilizing Cu in the hydrogenation reaction [11,29–32].
In our previous work, the production of CH3OH from CO2 liquid phase electroreduction was evaluated at Cu2O–ZnO mixtures at different catalytic loadings and weight ratios. The results showed mass transfer limitations in the electroreduction of CO2 in liquid phase when using a filter-press electrochemical cell. Therefore, the primary objective of this study is to go a step further and
Please cite this article in press as: J. Albo, A. Irabien, Cu2O-loaded gas diffusion e J. Catal. (2015), http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.jcat.2015.11.014
overcome the limitations in CO2 transfer by applying GDEs with spray supported Cu2O and Cu2O/ZnO catalysts for the continuous electroreduction of CO2 in gas phase. Then, an evaluation of the influence of key variables on the CO2 electroreducion process (i.e. current density, electrolyte flow and CO2 gas flow) is conducted.
The efforts carried out in this work will help to achieve the scale-up of CO2 valorization processes and devices in continuous operation, enabling a shift to a sustainable energy economy and chemical industry.

sections.heading: 2.1. Preparation and characterization of the gas-diffusion electrodes
sections.text:
The procedure to prepare the Cu2O and Cu2O/ZnO GDEs has been described in detail previously [11]. Briefly, the procedure is as follows: Cu2O (Sigma Aldrich, particle size <5 lm, 97% purity) and ZnO particles (ACROS organic, <45 lm, 99.5%) were mixed with a Nafion dispersion 5 wt.% (Alfa Aesar) and isopropanol (IPA) (Sigma Aldrich), with a 70/30 catalyst/Nafion mass ratio and a 3% solids (catalyst + Nafion). The Cu2O–GDEs contain 1 mg cm 2 of metal particles. The catalyst loading was kept at 1 mg cm 2 of Cu2O and 1 mg cm 2 of ZnO for the Cu2O/ZnO electrodes. These catalytic loading and weight ratio were observed to be the optimal for the reaction under study [11]. The inks were airbrushed onto a porous carbon paper (TGP-H-60, Toray Inc.) and dried to get the electrodes. All electrodes were dried and rinsed with deionised water before use.
The EDX spectra and surface mapping confirmed the composition and uniform distribution of Cu2O–ZnO metal particles onto the carbon paper (see Fig. A in Supporting Information). Thus, it can be inferred that the dispersion of the particles by airbrushing minimizes the agglomeration of the particles, which may greatly affect the electrode performance [26,27,32]. Besides the SEM cross-sectional image of the GDE shows that the diffusion layer (carbon paper) and the catalytic layer (Cu2O–ZnO) combined with each other tightly and the metallic particles covered nearly the entire carbon fibers of the support (see Fig. B in Supporting Information).

sections.heading: 2.2. Electrochemical cell and experimental conditions
sections.text:
The components of the experimental setup have been described in detail elsewhere [13]. The electroreduction of CO2 was carried out at ambient conditions using a filter-press electrochemical cell (Micro Flow Cell, ElectroCell A/S) in continuous operation. The cell was divided in a catholyte and anolyte compartments by a Nafion 117 cation exchange membrane (0.18 mm). The membrane presented a phase-segregated structure that allows the selective transport of H+ ions from the anode to the cathode chamber with a low permeability to CH3OH [33]. The membrane was activated prior to use with hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) aqueous solution (5 wt.%) at 60 C for 2 h, then immersed in a sulfuric acid (H2SO4) aqueous solution (1 M) at 60 C for 2 h and, finally, abundantly rinsed with distilled water, following standard procedures [34].
The airbrushed Cu2O and Cu2O/ZnO-catalyzed papers were employed as the working electrodes (geometric area, A = 10 cm 2), together with a platinized titanium plate used as the counter electrode and a Ag/AgCl (sat. KCl) reference electrode. The GDEs were weighted before and after the experiments in a precision digital balance (Sartorius, M-Power). To do so, the cell was disassembled after the CO2 electroreduction tests and the samples were dried in a plate at 100 C for 10 min before weighting.
The cathode side of the reactor was fed with CO2 gas (99.99%) with a flow/area ratio ranging from Qg/A = 10 to 40 ml min 1 cm 2,
lectrodes for the continuous electrochemical reduction of CO2 to methanol,
adjusted by a rotameter. A 0.5 M KHCO3 (Panreac, >97% purity) aqueous solution is used as both, catholyte and anolyte. According to the specifications given by the supplier, the KHCO3 salt may contain K2CO3 (2.5%) and other impurities at extremely low levels (e.g. Cl, SO4, NH4, PO4 or Fe). The employ of aqueous electrolytes constituted by alkali cations (i.e. K+) and halide anions (i.e. HCO3 ) can provide the required protons involved in the reaction pathway and favor higher currents, related to their cation size an electronegativity [35,36]. The electrolytes were pumped from catholyte and anolyte tanks to the cell by two peristaltic pumps (Watson Marlow 320, Watson Marlow Pumps Group) at a flow rate ranging from Qe/A = 1 to 3 ml min 1 cm 2.
In this study, the filter-press electrochemical system possesses three inputs (catholyte, anolyte and CO2 separately) and two outputs (catholyte–CO2 and anolyte) for the electroreduction of CO2 in gas phase. Fig. 1 schematically represents the electrolytic GDE cell configuration for the electroreduction of CO2 supplied directly from the gas phase.
The experiments were performed at galvanostatic conditions (i.e. at a constant current density), using an AutoLab PGSTAT 302 N potentiostat (Metrohm, Autolab B.V.). The current density ranged from j = 5 to 40 mA cm 2 in the electrochemical experiments. Liquid samples were taken every 15 min from the catholyte tank with a total operational time of 90 min, where pseudo-stable values are obtained [11]. All the experiments were carried out at ambient conditions.
To quantify the concentration of each product in the liquid phase, the samples were analyzed by duplicate in a headspace gas chromatograph (GCMS-QP2010, Ultra Shimadzu) equipped with a flame ionization detector (FID). Compounds were separated on a DB-Wax 30 m 0.25 mm 0.25 lm column, with an injection and detector temperature of 250 C and 270 C, respectively. Helium was used as a carrier gas at a flow rate of 50 ml min 1. The identification of obtained products was further confirmed by headspace gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GCMS-N5975B) using a 60 m 250 lm 1.40 lm DB-624 capillary column. Three replicates were performed for each sample to obtain an averaged concentration of the formed products. The standard deviations of all the experiments were below 18.6%.
The performance of the electrochemical process is evaluated by the rate of product formation, r (i.e. product obtained per unit of cathode area and time), and the Faradaic efficiency, FE (i.e. selectivity of the reaction for the production of each product). The FE

sections.heading: 3.1. Continuous electroreduction of CO2 in a filter-press electrochemical cell
sections.text:
The electroreduction of CO2 at the Cu2O-based GDEs led predominantly to the formation of CH3OH, in accordance with those previous results at copper oxide surfaces [11,27,28]. Additionally, small quantities of C2H6O and C3H8O were also detected. Fig. 2 shows the course of the applied voltage, E, and formation rate, r, of the main liquid-phase product, CH3OH, over time for the CO2 electroreduction at both electrodes under ambient conditions.
From the figure, the required voltage, E, remains stable for the Cu2O/ZnO-based electrodes over the course of the 90 min of operation. In contrast, the Cu2O electrode required an increasing applied voltage to maintain a stable current (j = 10 mA cm 2), which may be related to the progressive detachment of catalyst particles from the GDE surface and the deactivation due to the exposure to concentrated CO2 gas [37,38]. The deactivation of the electrodes with time may be additionally explained by the deposition of organic/inorganic substances and metals ions, originally contained in the electrolyte, in the electrode surface, which may deteriorate the electrocatalytic activity, as demonstrated by Hori et al. when evaluating the electrochemical reduction of CO2 to CH4 and alcohols at 0.5 KHCO3 aqueous solutions prepared from reagents from different manufacturers [39].
The lower potentials needed for Cu2O–ZnO mixtures (E = 1.16 V vs. Ag/AgCl) in comparison with Cu2O-based GDEs (E = 1.25 to 1.50 V vs. Ag/AgCl) are in agreement with the higher cyclic voltammetry responses reported for Cu2O/ ZnO-based electrodes in comparison with those electrodes with deposited Cu2O particles, denoting the synergic effect of Cu2O and ZnO in the current–potential reduction response [11]. Moreover, the observed fluctuations in required voltages for both systems can be explained as bubbles are formed at the applied current (j = 10 mA cm 2).
Moreover, the rate of CH3OH formation, r, decreased for both electrodes as time went on, and then stabilizes uniquely for Cu2O/ZnO layers after 30 min of reaction at r = 4 10 5 mol m 2 s 1 until the end of the experiment. Probably, at the first experimental minutes, the electrolyte penetrated into the internal structure of the GDE, enlarging the contact area. This may explain

the enhanced reaction rate at 15 min of operation, indicating that the structure is sufficiently soaked and the three-phase liquid films had totally formed thoroughly the whole GDEs [40]. After this point, the GDE probably was to wet, limiting mass transfer to some extent and accumulating liquid-phase reaction products, which can partially block the electrode and reduce its electrochemically-active surface area [41–43]. Therefore, a gradual infiltration of electrolyte may be preferred for an enhanced CO2 conversion at GDEs.
Table 1 shows the catalyst weight of the Cu-based samples after 30, 60 and 90 min of CO2 electroreduction time. The total weight of catalyst placed in the carbon paper was 10 mg and 20 mg for Cu2O and Cu2O/ZnO-based electrodes, respectively.
The results may indicate that the deactivation observed in the Cu-based electrodes is more probably linked to the detachment of catalytic particles during operation, rather than the poisoning produced by the impurities contained in the electrolyte, although this effect may certainly influence the rate of deactivation. Besides, the data confirmed the more stable properties of Cu2O/ZnO surfaces in comparison with the Cu2O-based electrode, where the catalysts may be gradually peeled off from the carbon paper, which is a common phenomenon observed in GDE systems [15,37,44].
Besides, defects in the catalytic layer would likely assist tunneling and an increase in the unwanted hydrogen formation, due to easy access of water to catalytic sites. Therefore, a uniform and defect free catalyst layer is desired [16,24]. According to the results, it is expected that Cu2O/ZnO layer could remain and catalyze the CO2 electroreduction for over 20 h (if we consider the same particle detachment rate), since the total particle loss at 90 min was 1.4 mg of a total of 20 mg sprayed in the electrode. Overall, even if the Cu2O–based GDEs present an initial better performance for CH3OH formation, the utilization of Cu2O–ZnO mixtures is recommended for a continuous CO2 electrochemical conversion due to its stable properties with time.
The averaged formation rate for Cu2O/ZnO surfaces at 90 min of operation takes the value of r = 4.74 10 5 mol m 2 s 1, which is remarkably higher than that value reported in our previous work at Cu2O/ZnO particles deposited onto carbon papers (without the supply of CO2 gas), r = 3.17 10 5 mol m 2 s 1 [11]. Besides, the stable formation rate obtained at Cu2O/ZnO-based electrode is above those values previously reported for air-furnace oxidized Cu foils (r = 2.36 10 5 mol m 2 s 1) and electrochemical oxidized Cu foils (r = 2.78 10 5 mol m 2 s 1) at potentials ranging from 1.2 to 1.5 V vs. Ag/AgCl [24], but below the CH3OH formation rates reached at electrodes based on Cu2O deposited on stainless steel by thin film electrodeposition, r = 11.9 10 5 m 2 s 1, at 1.05 V vs. Ag/AgCl in a typical three-electrode cell containing a CO2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 aqueous solution [28].

sections.heading: 3.2. Key variables on the CO2 electroreduction process

sections.heading: 3.2.1. Influence of current density
sections.text:
Fig. 3 shows the quantitative information (r and FE) regarding
the liquid-phase product distribution at different current densities (j = 5–40 mA cm 2). FE was calculated considering 6 electrons step pathways of CO2 reduction to CH3OH, 12 electrons required per molecule of ethanol (C2H6O) and 18 to produce n-propanol (C3H8O). A constant electrolyte flow/area ratio (Qe/A) and gas flow/area ratio (Qg/A) of 2 and 20 ml min 1 cm 2, respectively, were applied in the tests. It may be noted that the carbon paper without supported metallic particles in its surface did not produce any measurable liquid product. Besides, liquid samples from the anolyte tank were analyzed and no liquid products were detected, which denoted a negligible crossover of reaction products through the membrane.
The figures show that the product distribution and process efficiency are on dependence of the current density applied. The system predominantly produces CH3OH, with C2H6O as the second main product (which is a difficult reaction with 12 electrons transfer required). The literature shows that the formation of C2H6O at Cu-based electrodes is not unexpected [9,45–50]. For example, Chi et al. [46] reported a good selectivity for the formation of C2H6O (FE = 15.5%) for CuO nanoparticles deposited on carbon papers when using a 0.2 M KHCO3 solution. Trace amounts of CH3OH and C3H8O were also detected. Ren et al. [48] recently reported the formation of C2 compounds (C2H6O and C2H4) on Cu2O films at various electrochemical potentials. The FE was in the range of 9–16% for C2H6O formation in a 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte. They hypothesized that CO2 is reduced through proton-electron transfer to give HCOO surface moiety, which can then hydrogenate to give H2O and CO (adsorbed) at the copper surface. These species can further hydrogenate to form CH4 or undergo intermolecular C–C bound formation (C1 dimerization/ hydrogenation) to yield C2HnO2 (n = 0–4), which is further reduced to C2H6O and C2H4. The Cu+ ions were postulated to be the catalytic active for reducing CO2 to C2 compounds. Besides, Li and co-workers demonstrated that Cu2O films could reduce CO to C2H6O with a FE of 43% [49]. The metal particles boundaries on the surface (with undercoordinated Cu atoms) of the films were suggested to be the driving forces for C1 dimerization to form C2 products. Moreover, Kuhl et al. [9] evaluated the electrochemical reduction of CO2 on a Cu surface across a range of potentials and observed a total of 16 different CO2 reduction products (including CH3OH, C2H6O and C3H8O). They discuss a scheme for the formation of multicarbon products and recognized that all the C2 and C3 products detected may have been produced via the dehydroxylation of an earlier, less reduced product in its enol or diol form. Therefore, they hypothesized that the chemistry to generate the wide range of multicarbon products may occur through an enollike surface intermediate, that desorb to convert to its diol and/or keton form. The presence of hydroxyl and/or carbonyl moieties in many of the C2 and C3 products suggests that the C–C coupling step occurs before at least one of the two carbon–oxygen bonds in CO2 is broken. In any case, the mechanisms involved in C–C coupling reactions to form C2 and C3 products are still unclear. It is also worth mentioning here the notable role of KHCO3 aqueous electrolyte in the reaction, since CO2 might bond to HCO3 and K+, generating intermediate species prior to its electrochemical reduction. The formation of HCO3–C bonds results in the weakening of C–O and the activation of CO2 and so, the electron transfer from the electrode to CO2 is facilitated. Therefore, high concentrations of HCO3 may be favorable to reach high current densities in the system and produce more reduced species [36]. Certainly, fur-

The results also suggest that the reaction conditions created in the GDEs may be able to vary product selectivity if we compare the results with those obtained at identical catalytic surfaces and reaction medium, but without CO2 supplied as gas, where CH3OH was the main product and only trace amounts of C2H6O were detected [11]. This is not exceptional if we consider those results obtained by Kas et al. for electrodes prepared with Cu nanoparticles for CO2 electroreduction to hydrocarbons [47,50]. They proved that identical electrodes could yield predominately CH4 and C2H4 depending on process conditions, such as the applied CO2 pressure, that can modify the conditions in the vicinity of the catalytic material. In theory, the GDE configuration changes CO2 transfer radically. Owing to the abundant pores in the GDEs, CO2 can diffuse to the electrode surface more conveniently than that from the bulk. Moreover, CO2 in the reaction can be obtained from CO2 (gas), rather that CO2 (aqueous) by use of GDEs, so that the concentration of CO2 (adsorbate) on the electrode surface can be increased [41] which probably may lead to the formation of more reduced species, altering the distribution of products from the reaction. It is also interesting to note the positive effects of supplying a CO2 gas flow through the electrode structure, whichmight provoke that
the liquid products diffuse more easily to the solution, avoiding the entrapment of liquid products into the porous structure of the carbon paper. All together would explain the higher overall FE in comparison with those values obtained in our previous study [11].
Fig. 3a and b reveal that the total rate of CO2 reduction to liquidphase products, rT, did not improve at current densities higher than j = 10 mA cm 2, where a maximum value of rT = 8.32 10 5 - mol m 2 s 1 and rT = 5.08 10 5 mol m 2 s 1 can be obtained at Cu2O and Cu2O/ZnO-based electrodes, respectively. In addition, the overall FET (the results of cumulative efficiencies for the formation of the different products) fell drastically as the current was increased from j = 10 to 40 mA cm 2. This may be explained as the additional current density applied is consumed by side reactions, such as the production of hydrogen (which competes with the electroreduction of CO2 to useful products) and may indicate an optimal electrocatalytic current density of j = 10 mA cm 2, where the overall efficiency values can be as high as FET = 54.8% and 31.4% for the Cu2O and Cu2O/ZnO-based surfaces, respectively.
Table 2 compares the product distribution and FE for CO2 conversion obtained in the present work with those previously obtained for the same materials in a CO2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 solution (without CO2 supplied as gas) [11]. The overall FE achieved for the conversion of CO2 demonstrated that the GDE with CO2 gas feeding to the electrocatalysts contributed to the high electrolysis efficiency, as compared to those results obtained at the identical electrodes when no CO2 as gas is supplied [11]. In particular, the reaction efficiency for CH3OH production can be increased from FE = 17.7% to 27.5% when CO2 is supplied as gas at Cu2O/ZnO-based electrodes, which may signify that GDEs are able to intensify the CO2 mass transfer in the system and increase the availability of CO2 on the active catalytic surface of the materials. Despite that, the FE for the formation of CH3OH remains practically invariable at Cu2O-based GDEs, which can be likely attributed to the limited stability of the metallic particles deposited on the electrodes when flowing CO2 as gas through their porous structure, as discussed above in Section 3.1. Besides, the Cu2O–GDE maintained a higher efficiency for CO2 reduction (FET = 54.8%) at higher current density (j = 10 mA cm 2) than at Cu2O-surfaces (FET = 45.7%) at lower current applied (j = 6.93 mA cm 2). This may indicate that the application of GDEs (with CO2 supplied as gas) is advantageous, since the process can be operated at higher current densities, while yielding higher CO2 reduction efficiencies. Moreover, the efficiency values for the conversion of CO2 at GDEs are remarkably higher than those values obtained at a CO2-saturated solution when N2 gas is supplied through the GDE structure, which suggest that the conversion of CO2 molecule can be not uniquely attributed to an enhanced agitation and diffusion of reactants in the electrochemical cell, but also to an increase of CO2 (adsorbate) available on the catalytic surface, leading to more reduced species.

sections.heading: 3.2.2. Influence of electrolyte flow rate (Qe/A) and gas flow rate (Qg/A)
sections.text:
In order to improve the CO2 electroreduction performance, additional experiments were carried out at different electrolyte flow/area ratio (Qe/A) and CO2 gas flow/area ratio (Qg/A) and the results for the formation of the major product, CH3OH, are presented in Fig. 4a and b, respectively.
First, Fig. 4a shows that increases in Qe/A from 1 to 3 ml min 1 - cm 2 did not produce a significant alteration in the rate of CO2 electrochemical conversion to CH3OH, which indicated that using low Qe/A ratios is preferred in the GDE system since a more concentrated product can be obtained without sacrificing the rate of CH3OH formation (i.e. from 4.56 to 2.74 mg l 1 at Qe/A = 2 and 3 ml min 1 cm 2, respectively, at Cu2O/ZnO GDEs). Besides, lower electrolyte flows may allow a gradual infiltration of catholyte in the GDE structure, which is preferred for an enhanced CO2 electroreduction, as discussed in Section 3.1. Therefore, since process performance was only slightly affected by the electrolyte flow, it can be concluded that the process may be primarily limited by

Additionally, Fig. 4b demonstrates the importance of adjusting the optimal CO2 gas flow process. The lower formation rate (r = 2.48 10 5 mol m 2 s 1) for Cu2O/ZnO-based electrode at Qg/A = 10 ml min 1 cm 2 in comparison with that value at Qg/A = 20 ml min 1 cm 2 (r = 4.74 10 5 mol m 2 s 1) indicated that the process is clearly limited by the CO2 gas supplied to the system. On the other hand, the application of a high CO2 gas flow of Qg/A = 40 ml min 1 cm 2 produced a severe decrease in the formation rate for both electrodes, which can be mainly attributed to the rapid detachment of metal particles at these relatively high gas flows applied (41% and 22.5% catalyst weight losses for Cu2O and Cu2O/ZnO GDEs, respectively, after 90 min of operation), which led to a drastic current–potential reduction response during the operation time. Therefore, the optimal point should provide enough CO2 gas supply for the reaction, well before a massive detachment of metal particles occurs. This seems to happen at a flow range between Qg/A = 20 and 30 ml min 1 cm 2. These results are interesting and should be taken into account in order to design efficient processes for CO2 eletroreduction to CH3OH at GDE-based systems.

sections.heading: 3.3. Comparison with other electrocatalytic materials
sections.text:
Finally, the results obtained in the present work for Cu2O and Cu2O/ZnO–GDEs are compared with previous results for CO2 electroreduction to liquid products at different Cu-based materials (when boht, r and FE, values available) at an applied potential range of E = 1 to 1.5 V vs. Ag/AgCl [11,24,28,32]. Fig. 5 represents the total rate of CO2 conversion, rT, vs. cumulative Faradaic efficiency, FET, reported in the literature for the formation of different liquid-phase products, including CH3OH. The figure uniquely provides a picture for comparison of CO2 electroreduction performance, although other variables such as reaction medium, operating conditions and/or cell/electrode structure were applied, which may certainly affect the results [7]. The extraordinary high FE (i.e. >100%), where obviously both chemical and electrochemical steps are involved in the CO2 reduction process, obtained at anodized Cu foils and pre-oxidized Cu–TiOX electrodes [24] has been not included in order to clarify the analysis.
As can be seen from the figure, the total CO2 conversion efficiency obtained for GDEs in the present work outperformed those values observed at Cu, oxidized Cu and Cu–Zn surfaces, which may denote the positive effect of using GDEs. Nevertheless, the rate of CO2 reduction to useful products is still below those values reported for Cu2O electrodeposited-steel electrode, rT = 11.9 10 5 mol m 2 s 1 at 1.05 V vs. Ag/AgCl [28] or those values for Cu nanoclusters-ZnO mixtures at 1.4 V, where high

In any case, the relatively high CO2 conversion rate to liquid products, rT = 5.08 10 5 mol m 2 s 1 and total Faradaic efficiency, FET = 31.4%, as well as the stable behavior, suggests the use of Cu2O/ZnO-based-GDEs for the continuous electrochemical reduction of CO2 to useful products, where CH3OH is the predominant product. In addition, the stable efficiency values remarkably enhance the maximum CO2 conversion efficiency obtained in our previous work (FE = 17.7%) at Cu2O/ZnO catalysts, where no extra CO2 is provided as gas.
Future research should include the development of highly active catalysts for the reduction of CO2 at lower overpotentials. The development of new complex catalysts, catalyst assemblies, hybrid metal catalysts, nanostructures and Metallic Organic Frameworks (MOFs) will probably push the electroreduction technology closer to efficiencies for real applications [7]. It is also a key to understand the relationship between GDE morphology (e.g. surface area, number and accessibility of actives sites or support porosity) and an effective gas–liquid separation, in order to facilitate the diffusion pathways of reactants/products and lead to faster kinetics. These progresses may lead in the future to an economically viable CO2 electrochemical process to produce CH3OH in continuous operation.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text:
This work demonstrated that the electroreduction of CO2 gas to liquid products can be effectively carried out continuously in a filter-press electrochemical cell equipped with Cu2O and Cu2O/ZnO-based gas-diffusion electrodes (GDEs) in 0.5 M KHCO3 aqueous solution under ambient conditions. The GDE configuration allows breaking through the mass transfer limitations usually found in electroreduction systems, producing an enhanced CO2 reduction performance. The study included the experimental evaluation of key variables (i.e. current density, j; electrolyte flow/area ratio, Qe/A; and CO2 gas flow rate/area ratio, Qg/A) for the electrochemical reduction of CO2.
The experimental results in the filter-press electrochemical cell revealed that Cu2O/ZnO–GDEs are expected to remain stable over 20 h, in contrast to Cu2O surfaces that suffered a strong deactivation with time. The analysis of the liquid catholyte demonstrated that methanol was formed predominantly, with small amounts of ethanol and n-propanol.
The overall rate for the formation of liquid-phase products did not improve at current densities higher than j = 10 mA cm 2,
Please cite this article in press as: J. Albo, A. Irabien, Cu2O-loaded gas diffusion e J. Catal. (2015), http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.jcat.2015.11.014
where a maximum value of rT = 5.08 10 5 mol m 2 s 1 was obtained at Cu2O/ZnO–GDEs. In addition, the overall FE fell drastically as the current was increased from j = 10 to 40 mA cm 2. The performance was not affected by electrolyte flow, suggesting that the process may be primarily limited by the internal diffusion of reactants through the porous GDE structure, where the metal particles are deposited. In addition, the results demonstrated the importance of adjusting the optimal CO2 gas flow in the electrochemical cell in order to supply enough CO2 to react before a rapid detachment of metal particles from the catalytic surface occurred. Thus, the maximum efficiency detected at Cu2O/ZnO surfaces was FET = 31.4% (at j = 10 mA cm 2, Qe/A = 2 ml min 1 cm 2 and Qg/ A = 20 ml min 1 cm 2), which is a significantly higher value than those results previously reported in the literature for Cu-based electrodes and shows the potential of Cu2O/ZnO–GDEs for the effective electrochemical valorization of CO2.
Hence, the results presented in this work are promising, but research efforts must be continued in order to develop new electroreduction systems based on highly active, selective and stable materials to overcome the current limitations of the process before practical applications.
